key_claims: CSF low-frequency oscillations increase with time spent awake.
CSF low-frequency oscillations exhibit diurnal fluctuations, peaking in the early morning.
CSF low-frequency oscillations are strongly associated with vigilance and activity of the reticular activating system.
CSF low-frequency oscillations are not associated with plasma norepinephrine levels.
The observed changes in CSF low-frequency oscillations are not explained by EEG slow wave activity.
Time awake and diurnal time independently modulate vasomotion.
limitations: The study is a preprint and has not been peer-reviewed.
The study involved a 34-hour sleep deprivation protocol, which may not reflect normal sleep-wake patterns.
The study used healthy individuals, so findings may not generalize to clinical populations.
The study measured CSF oscillations indirectly via fMRI and NIRS, which may not directly measure vasomotion.
what_not_to_say: The study proves that sleep deprivation causes increased CSF oscillations.
The study shows that norepinephrine levels are unrelated to CSF oscillations in all contexts.
The study identifies a causal mechanism for CSF oscillations.
The study provides clinical recommendations for sleep or brain clearance.
The study demonstrates that wake-promoting nuclei directly drive CSF oscillations.
